result:
There's something quietly profound about watching steam rise from a cup of tea. It seems like nothing—just warmth escaping into air—but it's actually time made visible. The heat leaving your cup is the same one-way traffic that governs everything: stars burning out, ice melting, memories fading. Physicists call it entropy, but really it's just the universe forgetting how to be organized.

What strikes me is that we live entirely inside this flow without noticing. Every moment you experience is slightly warmer than the next, slightly more ordered than what follows. You are, in a sense, always standing at the top of a waterfall, and the water only goes down.

And yet—this is the part that gets me—life exists precisely because of that downhill rush. Plants eat sunlight and build sugar; animals eat sugar and build thought. We're not separate from entropy; we're eddies in it, little whirlpools that spin up complexity by borrowing energy and paying it back as heat. Every conversation you've ever had was powered by dissipated sunlight.

So when your tea goes cold, it isn't a small tragedy. It's the universe doing exactly what it does: spreading energy around, making room for new arrangements. You drink the tea while it's hot because you're alive, and you're alive because somewhere, a star is spending itself down. The cold cup at the end is just the receipt.

Maybe that's worth remembering the next time you wrap your hands around something warm: you're holding borrowed fire, and the borrowing is the whole point.
